title: How Many Yards of Gravel for a 20x20 Area?
description: A 20x20 ft area at 3 inches deep needs 3.7 cu yd of gravel, or 5.19 tons. At 4 inches deep it needs 4.94 cu yd, or 6.91 tons. Here is how to work it out.

sources.title: Mulch Pros: Material weight and coverage

body.text: A 20x20 foot area needs 3.7 cubic yards of gravel at 3 inches deep, or 4.94 cubic yards at 4 inches deep. At the default weight of 1.4 tons per cubic yard, that is 5.19 tons at 3 inches and 6.91 tons at 4 inches. Gravel is usually sold by the ton or the cubic yard, so check which unit your supplier uses before you order.

You can run your own numbers in the [Gravel & Sand Calculator](/gravel-calculator). Enter your length, width, depth and the weight per cubic yard, and it returns the volume and tonnage. The example below uses a 20x20 foot area, but the same steps work for any rectangle.
The short answer for a 20x20 area
The depth is the number that changes the order most. Here are the two common depths for this area:

items: 3 inches deep: 400 sq ft, 100 cu ft, 3.7 cu yd, which is 5.19 tons
4 inches deep: 400 sq ft, 133.3 cu ft, 4.94 cu yd, which is 6.91 tons

body.text: The area is the same in both rows. Only the depth changes, and the extra inch adds about 1.72 tons to the order.
How the calculation works
Gravel is measured by volume first, then converted to weight. The steps are the same for any area:

items: Find the area. A 20 ft length times a 20 ft width gives 400 sq ft.
Convert depth to feet or use the inch formula. Depth in inches is divided by 12 to get feet. At 3 inches, the volume is 400 sq ft times 3 in, divided by 12, which gives 100 cu ft.
Convert cubic feet to cubic yards. Divide by 27, since one cubic yard is 27 cubic feet. That gives 3.7 cu yd at 3 inches.
Convert cubic yards to tons. Multiply by the weight per cubic yard. The calculator default is 1.4 tons per cubic yard, which gives 5.19 tons at 3 inches.
Repeat with 4 inches. The volume becomes 133.3 cu ft, or 4.94 cu yd, and the weight becomes 6.91 tons.

body.text: A shortcut for cubic yards is area in square feet times depth in inches, divided by 324. For 400 sq ft at 3 inches, that is 400 x 3 / 324, which equals the 3.7 cu yd shown above. The calculator uses this same formula, so you get the same answer either way.
Why depth changes the order more than area
Gravel depth is easy to underestimate. Going from 3 inches to 4 inches looks like a small change, but it adds about a third more material. Here is what that means in practice:

items: At 3 inches, you order 3.7 cu yd, or 5.19 tons.
At 4 inches, you order 4.94 cu yd, or 6.91 tons.
The 20x20 area stays at 400 sq ft in both cases, so the extra material comes entirely from depth.

body.text: Before you choose a depth, confirm what the surface is meant to do. A thin decorative layer often uses less depth than a path or drive that carries foot or vehicle traffic. The calculator only estimates quantity. It does not tell you what depth your project needs, so pick a depth based on how the area will be used.
Cubic yards or tons: which should you order?

Many landscape and gravel suppliers sell by the ton, while bagged or small-quantity gravel is sold by weight or volume. Some bulk yards quote by the cubic yard. Ask which unit the quote uses before you compare prices.

The weight per cubic yard matters. The calculator default is 1.4 tons, or 2,800 lb, per cubic yard. Supplier tables list most gravel at about 2,600 to 2,800 lb per cubic yard, so the tonnage can shift depending on the stone. Ask your supplier for the weight of the specific product, then enter it in the calculator. If the supplier's weight is lower than 1.4 tons per cubic yard, the tonnage will go down for the same volume.
For a more detailed look at the conversion, see [Cubic Yards to Tons: How Much Gravel Weighs Per Cubic Yard](/blog/cubic-yards-to-tons-gravel).
Common mistakes when ordering gravel

items: Mixing up inches and feet. Depth must be in inches for the formula above. A 3-inch layer is not 3 feet.
Forgetting that cubic yards and tons are different units. A tonnage order will not match a cubic yard order without the right weight per cubic yard.

Ordering exactly the calculated amount. Gravel compacts and spreads unevenly, and ground is rarely perfectly flat. Many people order a little extra, then decide how much to add based on the area after the first load.
Using an unverified weight. The default weight is a starting point. Confirm it with the supplier before you order.

body.text: Also check the product label or the supplier's spec sheet for weight and coverage information. Products differ, and the figures on the label are the ones to trust for your order.

If you are planning a longer surface, the example in [How Much Gravel for a Driveway? 12x50 Example in Tons](/blog/how-much-gravel-for-driveway-12x50) shows the same steps for a larger area. For a smaller surface with a different material, see [How Much Pea Gravel for a 10x10 Area? Tons and Cubic Yards](/blog/how-much-pea-gravel-for-10x10-area).
Use the calculator for your own measurements

Measure your length and width in feet, choose a depth in inches, and enter the weight per cubic yard from your supplier. The [Gravel & Sand Calculator](/gravel-calculator) will show the volume in cubic yards and the weight in tons. Measure twice, because a small error in length or width changes the result.
FAQ
Is 3.7 cubic yards enough for a 20x20 area at 3 inches?

The calculator gives 3.7 cu yd for a 20x20 ft area at 3 inches deep. That is the volume for a level, even layer. Irregular ground or compaction can change how much you need, so compare this figure with your own site before ordering.
Why does 4 inches need so much more gravel than 3 inches?
The area stays the same, but the volume grows with depth. At 4 inches, the calculator gives 4.94 cu yd instead of 3.7 cu yd, and 6.91 tons instead of 5.19 tons.
What if my gravel weighs less than 1.4 tons per cubic yard?

Enter the weight from your supplier's spec sheet in the calculator. Supplier tables list most gravel at about 2,600 to 2,800 lb per cubic yard, so the tonnage may be lower than the default. Always confirm the weight with the supplier before you place the order.
